questions.q: What does a "gini impurity" of 0.0 at a leaf node mean?
options: The node has no training samples at all
Every sample that reaches that leaf belongs to the same class
The tree has not finished training
The feature used at that node is irrelevant
questions.explain: Gini impurity measures how mixed the classes are at a node; 0.0 means the node is perfectly pure — every sample there belongs to a single class.

questions.q: Why do decision tree decision boundaries look "boxy" (made of rectangles) rather than diagonal or curved?
options: Because trees can only be trained on two features
Because every split tests exactly one feature against one threshold, producing a straight line perpendicular to one axis
Because trees always use gradient descent
Because gini impurity forces curved boundaries
questions.explain: Each node's question compares one feature to a threshold, which is a straight line perpendicular to that feature's axis — stacking many such splits only ever produces rectangular regions.

questions.q: Why is an unconstrained single decision tree particularly prone to overfitting?
options: It cannot be trained on numeric features
With no depth limit, it can keep splitting until it carves out tiny regions to fit individual noisy examples
It always underfits instead
It requires more labeled data than any other model
questions.explain: A tree with no depth limit will keep splitting to reach perfectly pure leaves, which can mean creating a tiny, oddly-shaped region just to correctly classify one or two unusual training examples — memorizing noise rather than the real pattern.

questions.q: How does a Random Forest reduce the overfitting risk of a single tree?
options: By training one very deep tree instead of several shallow ones
By training many trees on random subsets of data and features, then averaging or voting across them
By removing all randomness from training
By using only linear splits instead of tree splits
questions.explain: Random Forest trains many trees, each on a random subset of training data and features, and combines their predictions — an individual tree's overfit quirks tend to get outvoted by the rest.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff when moving from a single decision tree to an ensemble like a Random Forest or gradient boosting?
options: Ensembles are always less accurate than a single tree
Ensembles typically improve accuracy and robustness but lose the single tree's easy, rule-by-rule readability
Ensembles can only be used for regression, never classification
There is no tradeoff; ensembles are strictly better in every way
questions.explain: Ensembles usually boost accuracy and robustness over a single tree, but you can no longer point to one simple, human-readable rule and say exactly why a prediction was made.
